articles.headline: Our cities are not built for the heat they now face
articles.standfirst: Heat action plans have saved lives. But a city where millions sleep under tin roofs and work in the open sun needs more than advisories and water kiosks.
articles.hero_caption: An illustration of a construction worker resting in the thin shade of a scaffold under a white-hot sky.
articles.hero_alt: Illustration of a labourer sheltering from harsh sun on a building site.

body.value:
There is a particular kind of silence that settles over an Indian city at three in the afternoon in May. Streets empty, shutters come halfway down, and the only people still out are those who have no choice: the construction worker on the eighth floor of an unfinished tower, the traffic constable, the woman selling cut fruit under a plastic sheet, the delivery rider racing a ten-minute promise. For them, the heat is not weather. It is a working condition.

We have become better, in some ways, at responding to it. Ahmedabad's heat action plan, the first of its kind in South Asia, showed more than a decade ago that early warnings, hospital preparedness and simple public messaging could reduce deaths during heatwaves. Dozens of cities and states now have similar plans, encouraged by the National Disaster Management Authority, and the India Meteorological Department issues heat warnings with far greater accuracy and lead time than it once did. These are real achievements, and the people who built them deserve credit.

But a heat action plan is, at heart, an emergency protocol. It tells people when to take shelter and tells hospitals when to expect patients. It does not change the fact that a family in a one-room tenement with a tin roof has no cool place in which to shelter, or that a daily-wage worker who stops between noon and four loses a third of the day's wage. It does not cool the city.

value.quote: A heat action plan tells people to stay indoors. It does not ask what indoors is like.

body.value:
Three changes would make a larger difference. The first is to treat heat as a labour issue. Several states have issued advisories asking employers to shift outdoor work away from the hottest hours, but advisories are not enforceable, and those who ignore them face no penalty. A binding rule on working hours during declared heatwaves, with compensation for lost hours for the lowest-paid, would protect people far better than a poster asking them to drink water. Some women's cooperatives have experimented with insurance that pays out automatically when temperatures cross a threshold; such schemes deserve public support and wider trials.

The second is to build differently. Cool roofs — a coat of reflective paint, or a modular insulating layer — can bring indoor temperatures down by several degrees at very low cost. Telangana has adopted a cool-roof policy, and pilot programmes in Ahmedabad and elsewhere have shown what is possible. Building codes, which still treat heat as an afterthought, should require passive cooling in new construction, and slum-upgrading programmes should take roofs as seriously as toilets.

The third is to plan for shade and water as public goods. Our cities have been paving over lakes and felling trees for road-widening for decades, and every one of those decisions has made the city hotter. Restoring tree cover along streets where people walk and wait, protecting water bodies, and keeping public drinking-water points working through the summer are not luxuries. They are infrastructure.

None of this is glamorous, and none of it fits neatly within a single department. Heat falls between the cracks of urban development, labour, health and disaster management, and so it is everyone's problem and nobody's responsibility. Some have argued that heatwaves should be formally notified as a disaster, which would unlock dedicated funds. That would help, but only if the money goes into prevention rather than relief after the fact.

Climate projections leave little doubt that hot days will become hotter and more frequent across much of India. We can keep responding to each summer as if it were a surprise, counting the dead and issuing advisories. Or we can start designing cities in which the people who keep them running can survive the afternoon.

articles.headline: Consent is not enough: the flaw at the heart of India's data protection rules
articles.standfirst: The new data protection regime asks individuals to read, understand and police how their data are used. That is a burden few can carry, and the law should not pretend otherwise.
articles.hero_caption: An illustration of a hand hovering over an endless scroll of privacy terms on a phone screen, with an 'I agree' button at the bottom.
articles.hero_alt: Illustration of a phone showing a very long privacy notice and an agree button.

body.value:
Somewhere in the settings of your phone are dozens of permissions you granted without reading: to a food-delivery app, a bank, a ride-hailing service, a game your child downloaded. Each came with a privacy notice you scrolled past. Under India's Digital Personal Data Protection Act and the rules that put it into effect, each of those taps is meant to carry legal weight. That is the problem.

The law is a genuine step forward. For the first time, Indians have a statutory right to know what personal data a company holds about them, to have it corrected or erased, and to complain to a Data Protection Board if their rights are violated. Companies that suffer breaches must report them, and penalties for failures can run into hundreds of crores. Children's data receive special protection, with verifiable parental consent required before processing. After years of drafts and delays, these are not small things.

But the architecture of the law rests on consent, and consent, as it operates online, is something close to a fiction. Studies of how people interact with privacy notices consistently find that almost nobody reads them, and that those who try rarely understand them. A regime that treats a tick in a box as informed agreement places the burden of protection on the individual — the party with the least information and the least power in the transaction.

value.quote: We do not ask passengers to inspect the engine before boarding a plane. Why do we ask users to audit a data processor before opening an app?

body.value:
The rules attempt to address this with “consent managers”: registered intermediaries through which users can give, review and withdraw consent across services. The idea has merit, and India's experience with account aggregators in finance shows that such intermediaries can work. But consent managers make consent easier to manage, not more meaningful. If the choice is between agreeing to broad data use and not using a service at all, a better interface does not change the choice.

What is missing is a stronger set of obligations that apply regardless of consent. Well-regarded data protection laws elsewhere lean heavily on principles such as purpose limitation and data minimisation, which require companies to collect only what they need for a stated purpose and to use it only for that purpose. The Indian law gestures at these ideas, but the weight of enforcement falls on whether consent was obtained, not on whether the processing was reasonable.

Two other features deserve scrutiny. The first is the breadth of the exemptions available to the government. The state is the largest processor of personal data in the country, through its identity, welfare, tax and health systems, and the law allows the Centre to exempt its agencies from many obligations on grounds such as security and public order. Exemptions are not unusual in such laws, but they should be narrow, time-bound and subject to independent oversight.

The second is the Data Protection Board itself. Its members are appointed by the government, and its independence will depend heavily on how it is staffed and funded. A regulator that must adjudicate complaints against government departments needs to be visibly separate from them. Journalists and transparency campaigners have also warned that the law's amendment to the Right to Information Act could make it easier for officials to refuse information by citing privacy.

None of this is an argument against the law. It is an argument for treating it as a beginning. The rules will be revised; the Board will issue decisions; courts will interpret its ambiguities. At each of those points, the guiding question should be whether protection depends on what an ordinary person can reasonably be expected to do. If it depends on reading privacy policies, it will not protect anyone.

articles.headline: Mumbai's lifeline needs more than automatic doors
articles.standfirst: Closing the doors on suburban trains will save some lives. The deaths will not stop until the railways tackle the crush that pushes people to the edge in the first place.
articles.hero_caption: An illustration of a crowded Mumbai suburban train at a platform, commuters packed into the open doorway.
articles.hero_alt: Illustration of an overcrowded local train with passengers at the door.

body.value:
Anyone who has taken a Mumbai local at 9.15 in the morning knows the choreography. You wait at the exact spot on the platform where the door will stop. You brace as the train pulls in, still moving. You are carried in by the crowd behind you, or you are not carried in at all, and you hang from the door frame with one hand and your bag clutched in the other, the wind tugging at your shirt as the train leans into a curve.

For millions of Mumbaikars this is not an adventure. It is the commute. The suburban network carries upwards of 70 lakh passenger journeys on a typical weekday, on rakes designed for a fraction of that load. The cost is measured in lives. For years, railway police records have counted deaths on the suburban tracks in the thousands every year — people falling from overcrowded trains, crossing tracks where no bridge exists, struck in the dark. The toll has declined from its worst, but every few months a single incident reminds the city how fragile the system remains.

After the most recent such tragedy, the railways said new suburban rakes would come with automatic doors, and that existing non-air-conditioned rakes would be retrofitted where possible. This is welcome. Closed doors will prevent some falls, and there is no good argument for running trains with open doors in this century. But we should be clear about what automatic doors can and cannot do.

value.quote: A closed door keeps people inside the train. It does nothing for the people left on the platform.

body.value:
On the busiest routes at peak hours, the crowd on the platforms of major stations already exceeds what a train can absorb. Doors that close will mean more people left behind, longer waits and heavier crowding on platforms and foot-overbridges, which carry risks of their own. Ventilation in non-AC trains with closed doors must be redesigned, or the cure will be worse than the disease in a Mumbai May. And none of this addresses deaths while crossing tracks, which have long made up a large share of the toll.

The real problem is capacity, and capacity is a decades-long project. Successive phases of the Mumbai Urban Transport Project have added lines, longer trains and new rakes, but implementation has repeatedly lagged behind schedule. Additional corridors to separate suburban from long-distance traffic, modern signalling that lets trains run closer together, and more fifteen-car services would each raise the number of people the system can carry safely. These are not new ideas. They have sat in reports for years.

There are cheaper levers too. Staggered office timings, which state and central government offices in the city could adopt tomorrow, would flatten the peak. Fencing and foot-overbridges at known crossing points would save lives at little cost. Better integration with the metro lines now opening across the city could draw passengers away from the most crowded stretches — but only if fares, ticketing and interchanges are designed for people switching modes, rather than as separate systems that happen to meet.

Air-conditioned trains, which come with automatic doors, deserve a word. They are popular with those who can afford them and resented by those who cannot, particularly when they replace ordinary services rather than adding to them. Safety should not become a premium product. Whatever is done must be done on the trains that most people actually ride.

Mumbai has learned to live with its local trains the way one learns to live with a chronic condition: with stoicism, humour and an elaborate set of coping habits. That resilience is admirable. It should not be mistaken for consent. The people who hang from the doors every morning are not taking a risk they chose. They are taking the only train there is.

articles.headline: Let Parliament do its homework
articles.standfirst: A crowded legislative agenda is no excuse for skipping scrutiny. Committees exist to slow good bills down just enough to make them better.
articles.hero_caption: An illustration of a committee room with members seated around a horseshoe table, bound reports stacked before them.
articles.hero_alt: Illustration of a parliamentary committee meeting around a horseshoe-shaped table.

body.value:
The government arrives at the monsoon session with a long list of bills and a short calendar. The opposition arrives with its own list of grievances. If past sessions are any guide, the outcome is predictable: days lost to adjournments, followed by a rush in the final week in which bills are passed in minutes, sometimes by voice vote amid protest. Both sides will then blame the other. Both will be partly right.

The casualty is scrutiny, and it is worth being precise about why that matters. Most laws are not passed to make headlines. They are technical instruments — on insolvency, cooperatives, shipping, the repeal of obsolete statutes — whose effects depend on definitions, exceptions and the powers they grant to officials. Errors in such details tend to surface years later, in courtrooms and in the lives of the people the law was meant to help. By then, correcting them requires another bill.

Parliament has a mechanism designed to catch those errors: its committees. Department-related standing committees and select committees can examine a bill clause by clause, take evidence from experts and affected groups, and propose amendments away from the theatre of the floor. Their proceedings are not televised, which allows members to change their minds without losing face. Many committee reports are models of careful, cross-party work.

Yet the share of bills referred to committees has fallen sharply over the past two decades, according to data compiled by PRS Legislative Research. Governments of different stripes have found it convenient to bypass a step that takes time and can produce awkward recommendations. That is a mistake, and not only on principle. Bills that have been through committee tend to be better drafted, command broader support and are less likely to be challenged in court.

value.quote: A committee referral is not a delay. It is quality control.

body.value:
We would urge three things this session. The government should refer at least the more complex bills on its list to committees, even at the cost of passing them in a later session. The opposition should allow question hour and legislative business to proceed, and use the debates it has demanded to argue its case rather than to disrupt. And the presiding officers should use the discretion the rules give them to send bills to committees where the government does not.

None of this is beyond reach. Parliament has worked better than this in the past and can again. The legitimacy of a law rests not only on the number of votes it receives but on the quality of the deliberation that produced it. Voters are entitled to expect that their representatives have read what they are voting for.

articles.headline: Bengaluru's water warning is meant for every city
articles.standfirst: The city's new rules on borewells and tankers are necessary. But the crisis they respond to is the product of decades of planning that treated water as someone else's problem.
articles.hero_caption: An illustration of a dried, cracked lake bed with apartment towers rising on its former shoreline.
articles.hero_alt: Illustration of a dry lake bed surrounded by high-rise buildings.

body.value:
Bengaluru's water board has announced rules to meter borewells, regulate private tankers and require builders to use treated wastewater. These are sensible measures, and overdue. But they are also an admission. A city that pumps much of its drinking water uphill from a river roughly a hundred kilometres away, and fills the gap by drilling ever deeper into a falling water table, has been living beyond its means for a long time.

The story is not unique to Bengaluru. Chennai's taps ran dry within recent memory. Delhi's poorer neighbourhoods depend on tankers every summer. Smaller cities growing at breakneck speed, from Telangana to Gujarat to the Gangetic plain, are reproducing the same pattern: development first, pipes later, groundwater in between.

That pattern has three features. Cities expand faster than their piped networks, so new neighbourhoods are built on borewells and tankers, which then become entrenched interests. The natural infrastructure that once stored and recharged water — lakes, wetlands, flood plains, open ground — is lost to construction, often with official sanction. And water is priced and measured so poorly that nobody, from the utility to the household, has an accurate picture of how much is used and how much is lost.

Each of these can be addressed. Metering, which Bengaluru is now extending to borewells, is the foundation: what is not measured cannot be managed. Treated wastewater, which most Indian cities still discharge into rivers and drains, can replace fresh water for construction, industry and landscaping on a large scale. Protecting and restoring water bodies is cheaper than building new reservoirs, and it reduces flooding in the monsoon — the other half of the urban water problem.

value.quote: A city that cannot account for its water cannot claim to manage it.

body.value:
The harder part is political. Water tariffs that reflect even a fraction of the cost of supply are unpopular; enforcement against errant tanker operators and illegal borewells antagonises powerful interests; protecting lakes means saying no to builders. Municipal bodies that have gone without elected councils for long periods, as many have, are especially poorly placed to make those choices with legitimacy.

None of this argues for waiting. Smart metering, wastewater reuse and lake restoration can begin within a single budget cycle, and they pay for themselves many times over in avoided tanker bills and flood damage. What they require is a municipal leadership willing to be accountable for water as a whole, rather than for pipes alone.

Bengaluru's new rules are a start. Every other growing city should read them not as a local story but as a forecast — and act before its own taps run dry.

articles.headline: India's women are working more. Look closely at what kind of work
articles.standfirst: Female labour-force participation has almost doubled in six years of official surveys. Most of the rise is in self-employment on farms and in family businesses, not in salaried jobs.
articles.hero_caption: An illustration of rising bars beside the silhouettes of women at work in a field, a shop and an office.
articles.hero_alt: Illustration of a rising bar chart with women working in a field, a shop and an office.

body.value:
For years, one statistic embarrassed every argument about Indian growth: fewer than a quarter of working-age women were in the labour force. In 2017-18 the government's Periodic Labour Force Survey (PLFS) put the figure at 23.3%, one of the lowest rates of any large economy. Six survey rounds later it stands at 41.7%. On paper, that is one of the fastest increases ever recorded anywhere.

You would expect such a leap to be front-page news, and in a way it has been. But the headline number hides more than it reveals. Dig into the survey's own tables and a more complicated picture emerges, one that should temper both the celebration and the scepticism.

value.title: Women in the labour force, % of those aged 15 and over
value.source: Periodic Labour Force Survey annual reports, MoSPI
value.note: Usual status (principal and subsidiary activity). Survey years run July to June.

body.value: Where the rise came from

The first thing the tables show is geography. The increase is overwhelmingly rural. In towns and cities women's participation has crept up by a few points; in villages it has surged. The second is the type of work. The share of women workers who are self-employed has grown, and within that category a large group is classified as "helpers in household enterprises": women working on the family farm or in the family shop, usually without a wage of their own.

That is still work, and the survey is right to count it. A woman who tends the family's livestock contributes to output whether or not anyone pays her. But it is not the transformation that the phrase "women joining the workforce" conjures up: the move into factories, offices and services, with an independent income, that reshaped the economies of East Asia.

value.quote: A rise in participation is not the same as a rise in opportunity. The survey can tell you the first; you have to dig for the second.

body.value: Three explanations, not mutually exclusive

Economists offer three explanations. The optimistic one is that rural women are genuinely doing more paid and productive work, helped by better roads, self-help groups, cooking-gas connections that free up hours once spent gathering fuel, and cash-transfer schemes that give women a little capital. The pessimistic one is distress: when household incomes are squeezed, more family members pitch in, and some of the jump coincides with the pandemic years. The technical one is measurement: survey questions and enumerator practice can change how unpaid work is recorded.

The evidence supports a bit of all three. The rise began before the pandemic and continued after it, which argues against a pure distress story. But salaried employment for women has grown far more slowly than participation, which argues against a pure success story.

value.title: Key points
points: Women's labour-force participation rose from 23.3% in 2017-18 to 41.7% in 2023-24, according to the PLFS.
The increase is concentrated in rural areas and in self-employment, much of it unpaid work in family enterprises.
Regular salaried jobs for women have grown far more slowly.
The real test is whether women's earnings, not just their participation, keep rising.

value.title: How the PLFS measures work
value.body: The survey asks what each person did over the previous year ("usual status"). Someone counts as in the labour force if they worked, or sought work, for a major part of the year, or worked for at least 30 days in a subsidiary role. Unpaid helpers in a household enterprise count as workers. Since 2025 the survey has also published monthly and quarterly estimates, which are not directly comparable with the annual series shown here.

body.value: What to watch

The numbers that matter next are earnings and job type. If women's average earnings and their share of regular salaried work start to climb, the story of the past six years will look like the start of a genuine transformation. If they do not, India will have counted its women into the workforce without paying them for it.

sources.title: Periodic Labour Force Survey, annual reports 2017-18 to 2023-24
sources.publisher: Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation

articles.headline: The fertility map that could redraw Indian politics
articles.standfirst: Southern states have reached European birth rates; parts of the north have not. With a new census due, here is why that gap has become a constitutional question.
articles.hero_caption: An illustration of a map of India shaded in bands of colour, with a ballot box in the foreground.
articles.hero_alt: Illustration of a shaded map of India and a ballot box.

body.value: India's population story is usually told as one number. It is really two countries moving at different speeds. Most states now have fewer than 2.1 children per woman, the "replacement" rate at which a population eventually stops growing. A handful of large northern states are still above it. That gap, once a matter for demographers, now sits at the heart of a political argument about how many seats each state should have in Parliament.

value.title: Total fertility rate: children per woman, selected states
value.note: Replacement fertility is about 2.1 children per woman.

value.question: What is delimitation?
value.answer: Delimitation is the redrawing of constituency boundaries and the reallocation of seats among states according to population. The Constitution links each state's share of Lok Sabha seats to its population, so that one vote carries roughly the same weight everywhere.

value.question: Why has it not happened for so long?
value.answer: Seat shares were frozen on the basis of the 1971 census, first in 1976 and again by a constitutional amendment in 2001, which extended the freeze until the first census taken after 2026. The aim was to avoid penalising states that brought their birth rates down. That deadline is now in sight.

value.question: What changes with the next census?
value.answer: The census, the first since 2011, has a reference date of 1 March 2027, with snow-bound areas counted earlier. Once its figures are published, the freeze lapses unless Parliament extends it. A straightforward reallocation by population would shift seats from the south and east towards the populous northern states, because their populations have grown faster since 1971.

value.label: the census on which each state's share of Lok Sabha seats is still based

value.question: Why do southern states object?
value.answer: Their argument is one of fairness: they did what national policy asked, reducing fertility through education and health care, and would be rewarded with less political weight. They also point out that they contribute more in taxes than they receive from the Centre. Northern states reply that equal representation for every citizen is a basic democratic principle that cannot be frozen for ever.

value.question: Are there ways to soften the blow?
value.answer: Several have been floated: enlarging the Lok Sabha so that no state loses seats in absolute terms, extending the freeze again, or giving the Rajya Sabha a stronger role in protecting states' interests. Each has costs. A much larger House may be unwieldy; another freeze postpones a problem that grows with every decade.

value.title: Key points
points: Most states are below replacement fertility; Bihar, Uttar Pradesh and a few others are above it.
Lok Sabha seat shares are still based on the 1971 census.
The freeze on seat shares lasts until the first census after 2026, which has a reference date of 1 March 2027.
How Parliament handles reallocation will test Centre-state relations for a generation.

articles.headline: Ten minutes to your door: the costly arithmetic of quick commerce
articles.standfirst: Grocery delivery in minutes has become a fixture of Indian cities. Whether it can make money without hollowing out the neighbourhood kirana is still an open question.
articles.hero_caption: An illustration of a delivery rider on a scooter racing past a small neighbourhood shop, with a stopwatch overhead.
articles.hero_alt: Illustration of a delivery rider passing a corner shop beneath a stopwatch.

body.value:
Order a packet of curd, a phone charger and a bunch of coriander, and in many Indian cities they will be at your door before the kettle boils. Quick commerce, the business of delivering everyday goods in ten to twenty minutes, has gone from novelty to habit in barely four years. It is now the fastest-growing slice of Indian retail and one of the most fiercely contested.

The question investors keep asking is simple: can it make money? The question everyone else should ask is what it does to the 1.3 crore or so small shops that have supplied India's daily needs for generations.
The machine behind the minutes

The speed does not come from fast riders but from geography. Platforms run "dark stores": small warehouses, closed to the public, placed within two or three kilometres of their customers and stocked with a few thousand of the most-ordered items. The model works only where orders are dense enough to keep riders busy and stock moving, which is why it began in the biggest metros and is now pushing into smaller cities with mixed results.

The economics hinge on three numbers: how much each order is worth, how many orders each dark store handles a day, and how much the platform spends on discounts to win them. Platforms have worked hard on the first, adding electronics, beauty products and even appliances to lift basket size, and on the second by blanketing cities with stores. The third is where the money has gone.

value.quote: The ten-minute promise is a real-estate strategy disguised as a delivery service.

body.value: The kirana question

Distributors' associations have complained to the Competition Commission of India that deep discounting by well-funded platforms amounts to predatory pricing, and that brands give them better terms than traditional channels. The platforms reply that they are expanding the market, not stealing it, and that consumers clearly want what they offer.

Both can be partly true. The kirana's strengths (credit to regular customers, personal service, a shopkeeper who knows your order) are real, and many have adapted by taking orders on WhatsApp and delivering themselves. But the shops most exposed are those in dense, affluent neighbourhoods, where quick commerce is strongest and where margins on packaged goods were already thin.

value.title: Key points
points: Quick commerce depends on dense networks of dark stores close to customers.
Profitability turns on order value, orders per store and discount spending.
Distributors allege predatory pricing; platforms say they are growing the market.
Urban kiranas in affluent areas face the most pressure; many are adapting with their own delivery.

body.value: What to watch

Watch for three things: whether the platforms' reported losses keep narrowing as they cut discounts, whether the competition regulator opens a formal inquiry, and whether expansion into smaller cities holds up once the novelty fades. If density turns out to be a metro luxury, quick commerce will settle into being a large but limited business rather than the future of Indian retail.

articles.headline: Nine in ten lose: why SEBI keeps tightening the rules on derivatives trading
articles.standfirst: The market regulator's own study found that 93% of individual futures and options traders lost money over three years. Here is what it has changed, and why the losses have not disappeared.
articles.hero_caption: An illustration of a smartphone showing a jagged red trading chart, with coins slipping through an open hand.
articles.hero_alt: Illustration of a phone with a falling trading chart and coins slipping through a hand.

body.value: India has become the world's largest market for equity options by number of contracts traded, and much of that volume comes from individuals trading on their phones. In 2024 the Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI) published a study of what happened to them. The answer was stark, and it has driven a steady tightening of the rules ever since.

value.label: share of individual F&O traders who lost money between 2021-22 and 2023-24

value.question: What are futures and options?
value.answer: They are derivatives: contracts whose value depends on the price of something else, such as a share or an index like the Nifty. An option gives the right, but not the obligation, to buy or sell at a set price before a set date. Because a small payment controls a large exposure, gains and losses are magnified. Options that expire within days, popular with retail traders, are especially volatile.

value.question: What did SEBI find?
value.answer: Studying more than a crore of individual traders, SEBI found that 93% lost money over the three years to March 2024, with aggregate losses of more than ₹1.8 lakh crore. Only about one in a hundred made profits of more than ₹1 lakh after transaction costs. Much of the money flowed to proprietary trading firms and foreign investors using algorithms.

value.question: What has SEBI changed?
value.answer: From late 2024 it phased in a package of measures: a larger minimum contract size for index derivatives, so that each trade requires more capital; only one weekly expiry per exchange; collection of option premiums upfront; extra margin on expiry days; and an end to some margin benefits on calendar spreads. Exchanges were also told to monitor positions within the trading day.

value.question: Has it worked?
value.answer: Volumes fell after the changes, and the number of individual traders dipped. But a follow-up study found that the large majority of those still trading continued to lose money. Tightening the rules can make the casino smaller; it cannot change the odds for players up against faster, better-capitalised rivals.

value.title: Before you trade
value.body: Brokers must now show every client a risk disclosure based on SEBI's findings when they log in to trade derivatives. If you trade, compare your total profit and loss after brokerage, taxes and charges over a full year, not your best week.

value.title: Key points
points: SEBI's 2024 study found 93% of individual F&O traders lost money over three years.
Contract sizes, weekly expiries and margin rules have all been tightened.
Volumes fell, but most remaining retail traders still lose money.

articles.headline: Ahmedabad 2030: what the Commonwealth Games can, and cannot, buy India
articles.standfirst: The centenary Games will be India's first big multi-sport event since Delhi 2010. Done well, they are a rehearsal for an Olympic bid. Done badly, they are a repeat of 2010.
articles.hero_caption: An illustration of a stadium bowl at dusk with a running track and the outline of Ahmedabad's skyline.
articles.hero_alt: Illustration of a stadium at dusk against a city skyline.

body.value: When Ahmedabad was confirmed as host of the 2030 Commonwealth Games, the celebrations had a second audience in mind. The 2030 Games mark a hundred years since the first edition in Hamilton, Canada; for India's sports establishment they are also a dress rehearsal. The country has told the International Olympic Committee that it wants to host the 2036 Olympics, and Ahmedabad is the likely candidate city. Every venue, contract and traffic plan for 2030 will be read as evidence for or against that ambition.
The shadow of 2010

You do not have to be old to remember Delhi 2010. The Games themselves went off reasonably well, and Indian athletes won a record haul of medals. But the run-up was a cautionary tale: venues finished at the last minute, costs far above early estimates, and corruption cases that dragged on for years. An official inquiry catalogued delays and irregularities in contracts. The phrase "Commonwealth Games" became, for a while, shorthand for waste.

The organisers of 2030 have every incentive to show that lesson has been learned. The Commonwealth Games movement itself has changed: the Glasgow 2026 Games were cut to a slimmer programme of sports, using existing venues, to keep costs down. Ahmedabad has the opposite temptation: to build big, because an Olympic bid rewards spectacle.

value.quote: A Games is a seven-year infrastructure project with a two-week party at the end. Judge it by the seven years.

body.value: What the Games can buy

Done well, a multi-sport event can leave behind useful things: public transport built to a deadline, training facilities that elite and young athletes can actually use afterwards, and an events industry that knows how to run competitions to international standards. It can also give Olympic sports outside cricket a rare moment in front of a mass audience.

What it cannot buy is a sporting culture. India's medal tally at the Olympics depends on what happens in schools, district stadiums and state federations, not in a showpiece arena. Spending on a few iconic venues can crowd out the dull, decentralised investment that produces athletes.

value.title: Key points
points: Ahmedabad will host the centenary Commonwealth Games in 2030.
India has signalled interest in hosting the 2036 Olympics; 2030 is a test run.
Delhi 2010's cost overruns and corruption cases are the benchmark to beat.
The lasting value lies in usable facilities and transport, not iconic stadiums.

body.value: What to watch

Three early signals will tell you how this is going: whether a published, audited budget appears and stays close to reality; whether venue plans include a credible use for each facility after 2030; and whether governance of the organising committee is transparent enough that procurement decisions can be scrutinised. Get those right and the Olympic case writes itself. Get them wrong and 2010 will not be the last cautionary tale.

articles.headline: After the World Cup, the hard part: building women's cricket below the summit
articles.standfirst: India's first women's ODI World Cup title brought crowds, sponsors and prime-time audiences. Turning one triumph into a deep, durable game depends on what happens far from the stadium lights.
articles.hero_caption: An illustration of a young girl in cricket whites practising in a dusty schoolyard, a floodlit stadium in the distance.
articles.hero_alt: Illustration of a girl practising cricket in a schoolyard with a stadium in the distance.

body.value:
When India beat South Africa in Navi Mumbai in November 2025 to win the women's ODI World Cup for the first time, the scenes looked familiar to anyone who remembered 1983 or 2011: crowded streets, overnight celebrations, cricketers turned household names. The comparison is apt in another way. Those men's triumphs did not just reward a generation; they reshaped the sport's economics.

Whether the women's win does the same depends less on the players at the top than on the structures beneath them.
What has already changed

The women's game in India has been building for some time. In 2022 the Board of Control for Cricket in India (BCCI) announced equal match fees for its centrally contracted women and men in international cricket. The Women's Premier League (WPL), launched in 2023, gave players franchise contracts, exposure to overseas teammates and a televised domestic stage. A World Cup win on home soil adds the one thing that money alone cannot buy: a mass audience that now knows the players' names.

value.quote: A trophy fills stadiums for a season. A pathway fills them for a generation.

body.value: Where the gaps are

Below the elite, the pathway thins quickly. Many girls still have no school or district team to play in, and the number of well-equipped grounds and qualified women coaches is small. The domestic calendar, though longer than it was, offers fewer matches and lower pay than the men's. Associations in some states treat the women's programme as an obligation rather than an investment.

None of this is unusual; women's sport everywhere has had to fight for the same basics. But India has an unusual opportunity: a governing body with enormous resources and, for the first time, commercial demand that justifies spending them.

value.title: Key points
points: India won its first women's ODI World Cup in November 2025.
Equal international match fees (2022) and the WPL (2023) laid the groundwork.
Grassroots access, coaching and the domestic calendar are the weak links.
Commercial demand now gives the board a business case for investing below the elite level.

body.value: What to watch

Measure success by numbers that are less glamorous than television ratings: how many girls are registered with state associations, how many domestic matches women play each year, and how many women coach and umpire. If those climb over the next five years, the 2025 team will have done more than win a trophy.

articles.headline: Why India keeps producing chess grandmasters
articles.standfirst: A country that had one grandmaster in 1988 now has more than 80, a world champion and Olympiad gold. Here is how that happened.
articles.hero_caption: An illustration of a chessboard with pieces casting long shadows shaped like a city skyline.
articles.hero_alt: Illustration of chess pieces casting shadows shaped like a skyline.

body.value: In 1988 India had exactly one chess grandmaster. Today it has more than 80, and in the space of a few months in 2024 it won both the open and women's gold medals at the Chess Olympiad in Budapest and produced the youngest undisputed world champion in the game's history. Few countries have climbed so far, so fast, in any sport.

value.label: Indian chess grandmasters, up from one in 1988

value.question: Where did it start?
value.answer: With Viswanathan Anand, who became India's first grandmaster in 1988 and later world champion. His success made chess a respectable career in a country where it had been a pastime, and it turned Chennai into the centre of Indian chess, with clubs, coaches and a culture of tournament play that fed generation after generation.

value.question: Why so many now?
value.answer: Three things came together. Strong computer engines and online platforms gave young Indians access to world-class training material and opponents without leaving home. A dense network of private academies and coaches, many of them strong players themselves, turned that access into systematic preparation. And a crowded calendar of open tournaments at home let promising juniors earn the rating points and title norms they need.

value.question: Does government support matter?
value.answer: It has helped at the margins: state governments, particularly Tamil Nadu, have backed tournaments and hosted the 2022 Chess Olympiad in Mamallapuram. Public-sector employers have long given sports quotas to strong players. But the engine of Indian chess has mostly been families and private coaches, which is also its weakness: the pathway favours children whose parents can afford coaching and travel.

value.question: What could slow it down?
value.answer: Cost and concentration. A few states produce most of the grandmasters, and the expense of international tournaments is a barrier for talented players from poorer families. Broadening the base, through school chess and travel grants, would decide whether this is a golden generation or a permanent fact of the chess world.

value.title: Key points
points: India has gone from one grandmaster in 1988 to more than 80.
In 2024 it won both Olympiad golds and produced the youngest undisputed world champion.
Engines, online play, private academies and a busy domestic calendar drove the rise.
Cost and regional concentration are the main obstacles to going further.

articles.headline: India's solar boom has a sunset problem
articles.standfirst: Clean sources now make up half of India's installed power capacity, years ahead of target. But demand peaks after dark, and without storage the sun cannot keep the lights on.
articles.hero_caption: An illustration of rows of solar panels in a desert at sunset, with a city lighting up on the horizon.
articles.hero_alt: Illustration of solar panels in the desert at sunset and a city lighting up beyond.

body.value:
In mid-2025 India passed a milestone it had promised the world for 2030: half of its installed electricity capacity now comes from non-fossil sources. Solar did most of the lifting, with installed capacity crossing 100 gigawatts earlier that year, more than ten times what it was a decade before. On a sunny afternoon, solar farms in Rajasthan and Gujarat now supply a large share of the country's power.

Then the sun sets, the air conditioners stay on, and the grid turns back to coal.

value.label: share of India's installed power capacity from non-fossil sources, reached in mid-2025
value.source: Ministry of New and Renewable Energy

body.value: Capacity is not electricity

The milestone measures capacity: how much power plants could produce at full tilt. Solar panels produce for only part of the day, so their share of electricity actually generated is far smaller than their share of capacity. Coal still supplies most of India's electricity, and it supplies almost all of it after dark.

That matters more each year because India's demand curve has changed. Peak demand, which used to come in the afternoon, increasingly arrives in the evening, when households switch on lights, fans and air conditioners. Grid managers call the shape the "duck curve": cheap solar floods the middle of the day, then expensive power has to ramp up quickly as the sun goes down.

value.quote: India has solved the problem of making cheap electricity at noon. The next problem is selling it at nine at night.

body.value: Storage, finally

The answer is storage, chiefly batteries and pumped hydro. Battery prices have fallen sharply, and recent government tenders for battery storage have drawn bids far below what was expected a few years ago. The Centre has offered viability-gap funding to support early projects, and the power ministry has advised that new solar tenders include storage alongside the panels.

The constraint is now less about technology than about rules and wires. Transmission lines from the sunny west have lagged behind new solar farms, leaving some capacity stranded. State distribution companies, many of them financially weak, are reluctant to sign long contracts for storage that costs more than the coal power they are used to.

value.title: Key points
points: Non-fossil sources reached half of installed capacity in 2025, years ahead of the 2030 goal.
Solar's share of electricity generated is much smaller than its share of capacity.
Evening peaks still depend on coal; storage is the missing piece.
Transmission and the finances of state discoms are now the binding constraints.

body.value: What to watch

Track how much storage is actually commissioned, not tendered; how fast new transmission corridors from Rajasthan and Gujarat are completed; and whether evening coal generation starts to flatten. Those are the numbers that will show whether India's clean-energy story extends past sunset.

articles.headline: India's carbon market, explained: who must cut, and who pays
articles.standfirst: Heavy industries now have legally binding targets to cut the carbon intensity of what they make. Here is how the new trading scheme works, and why Europe's border tax gives it extra urgency.
articles.hero_caption: An illustration of factory chimneys whose smoke turns into a rising and falling price chart.
articles.hero_alt: Illustration of factory chimneys with smoke shaped like a price chart.

body.value: India has a carbon market. Most people have not noticed, because it is designed to start slowly and because it does not cap total emissions. But for the country's aluminium smelters, cement kilns, paper mills and chlor-alkali plants, it is now the law, and it will soon reach steel and refineries too.

value.question: What is the Carbon Credit Trading Scheme?
value.answer: It is a framework notified in 2023 under the Energy Conservation Act, as amended in 2022. It has two parts: a compliance market, in which designated industrial plants must meet targets, and a voluntary market, in which others can earn credits for cutting emissions. The Bureau of Energy Efficiency runs it, with trading on power exchanges.

value.question: How do the targets work?
value.answer: Each obligated plant gets a target for greenhouse-gas emissions intensity: tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent per tonne of product. A plant that beats its target earns carbon credit certificates; one that misses must buy certificates from others or pay a penalty. Because the targets are about intensity, a plant can grow its output, and its total emissions, while still complying, provided each tonne it makes is cleaner.

value.question: Which industries are covered?
value.answer: Targets were first notified for aluminium, cement, chlor-alkali, and pulp and paper plants, with others, including petroleum refining, petrochemicals, textiles, and iron and steel, set to follow. These are among the most energy-intensive industries in the country.

value.question: Why does Europe matter?
value.answer: The European Union's Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM) puts a charge on the embedded emissions of imports such as steel, aluminium and cement, with payments due from 2026. Indian exporters may be able to deduct a carbon price paid at home. A credible domestic price could therefore keep money in India that would otherwise go to European treasuries.

value.question: Will it cut emissions?
value.answer: That depends on how tight the targets are and what certificates end up costing. Intensity targets that merely follow existing efficiency trends will produce a market with plenty of supply and a low price, rewarding plants for what they would have done anyway. Stricter targets would bite harder but raise costs for industries that employ millions.

value.title: Key points
points: India's compliance carbon market sets emissions-intensity targets, not an absolute cap.
Aluminium, cement, chlor-alkali and paper came first; steel and refining follow.
Plants that beat targets earn certificates; those that miss must buy them.
Europe's border carbon tax gives India a reason to establish a credible price.

articles.headline: Lost and found in translation: Indian fiction's quiet revolution
articles.standfirst: Two International Booker prizes in four years went to books translated from Indian languages. The real story is the translators, and the publishers finally paying them attention.
articles.hero_caption: An illustration of an open book whose pages turn into scripts from several Indian languages.
articles.hero_alt: Illustration of an open book with pages becoming Indian scripts.

body.value:
For most of its modern history, Indian literature reached the wider world in one language: English. Writers in Hindi, Bengali, Tamil, Malayalam, Kannada and a dozen other languages had vast readerships at home and almost none abroad. That is changing, and fast.

In 2022 the International Booker Prize went to Tomb of Sand, Geetanjali Shree's Hindi novel in Daisy Rockwell's translation. In 2025 it went to Heart Lamp, Banu Mushtaq's Kannada short stories translated by Deepa Bhasthi: the first collection of stories, and the first book translated from Kannada, to win. Two wins in four years is not a fluke. It is the visible tip of a shift in what Indian publishers commission and what readers buy.
The translator steps forward

The International Booker splits its prize equally between author and translator, and that principle is spreading. Translators' names increasingly appear on Indian book covers rather than in small print inside. Domestic prizes, notably the JCB Prize for Literature, have repeatedly honoured translated novels, giving publishers a commercial reason to look beyond English.

There is a practical side, too. A good translator is also a scout, an editor and an advocate, spotting books that could travel and persuading publishers to take a risk. Many of the translations now winning prizes began as passion projects that took years to find a home.

value.quote: For a century the question was which Indian writers wrote in English. Now it is which English readers will read Indian writers.

body.value: What still holds it back

Translation remains badly paid, and the pool of skilled translators for some language pairs is tiny. Most translation still flows into English, not between Indian languages: a Malayalam reader is more likely to find a Kannada novel in English than in Malayalam. And prizes concentrate attention on a few titles while the backlist of great untranslated work grows.

value.title: Key points
points: Translated Indian books won the International Booker in 2022 (Hindi) and 2025 (Kannada).
Translators are gaining recognition, prize money and cover credit.
Domestic prizes have given publishers a commercial reason to commission translation.
Pay, a shortage of translators and the dominance of English remain obstacles.

articles.headline: The single screen's last reel
articles.standfirst: The neighbourhood cinema hall built India's film culture. Squeezed by multiplexes, streaming and property prices, thousands have closed. A few are finding ways to survive.
articles.hero_caption: An illustration of an old art-deco cinema facade with a hand-painted poster and a single lit marquee bulb.
articles.hero_alt: Illustration of an art-deco cinema facade with a hand-painted poster.

body.value: Every Indian town had one: a hall with a hand-painted poster, a balcony that cost a little more, and a crowd that whistled at the hero's entry. Single-screen cinemas built the habit of moviegoing that made India the world's most prolific film industry. By most industry estimates, their number has fallen by more than half in the past two decades.
Three squeezes at once

The first squeeze was the multiplex. From the early 2000s, chains built screens in malls with better sound, comfortable seats and food that earns more than tickets. Urban audiences followed. The second was property: a single screen in the middle of a growing city often sits on land worth far more as a shopping centre or apartments than as a cinema. Owners who inherited a hall faced a simple calculation.

The third was streaming. Since the pandemic, films reach subscription platforms within weeks of release, and many mid-sized films skip cinemas altogether. For a hall that depends on a steady supply of films its audience wants, a thinner release calendar is fatal.

value.quote: A multiplex sells an evening out. A single screen sold a town its stories.

body.value: Who is surviving, and how

The survivors tend to share a few traits. Many are in smaller towns where multiplexes have not arrived. Some have renovated, adding better projection and seating while keeping prices low. Others have found loyal audiences for regional-language cinema, especially as big Telugu, Tamil, Malayalam and Kannada films have drawn crowds across the country. A few in big cities have become heritage venues, programming festivals and restored classics.

value.title: Key points
points: Single-screen cinemas have declined sharply over two decades.
Multiplexes, land values and streaming squeezed them at once.
Survivors rely on smaller towns, renovation, regional cinema and heritage programming.

body.value: What to watch

Policy can help at the margins: lower entertainment taxes for small halls, easier rules for converting part of a building while keeping the screen, and support for digital projection. But the decisive factor is the films themselves. As long as the industry makes films that work best in a packed, noisy hall, some halls will keep their lights on.

sources.title: Annual reports on the media and entertainment sector

articles.headline: UPI in one chart: from under a billion payments a year to 185 billion
articles.standfirst: India's instant-payments system has grown two-hundredfold in seven years. The curve is still rising, but the money behind it has a problem: almost nobody pays to use it.
articles.hero_caption: An illustration of a QR code dissolving into a steeply rising line of dots.
articles.hero_alt: Illustration of a QR code turning into a rising line of dots.

body.value: Few charts in Indian economic life look like this one. In the financial year 2017-18, the first full year of the Unified Payments Interface (UPI), Indians made fewer than a billion payments with it. In 2024-25 they made about 185 billion: roughly 500 million a day, from tea stalls to tax payments.

value.title: UPI transactions per financial year, billions
value.source: National Payments Corporation of India (NPCI), monthly UPI statistics
value.note: Financial years run April to March. Figures rounded.

body.value: Small payments, big numbers

The growth is mostly in volume, not value. The average UPI payment has been falling for years as people use it for ever smaller purchases: the vegetable vendor, the auto-rickshaw, the ₹20 cup of chai. That is exactly what its designers hoped for. Cash's great advantage was that it worked for tiny amounts; UPI has taken that advantage away.

value.quote: UPI has become public infrastructure, like a road. The question is who pays to resurface it.

body.value: The money problem

Because the government has set a zero merchant discount rate for most UPI payments, banks and payment apps earn almost nothing directly from processing them. The system is funded by a mix of government incentives and the hope of cross-selling loans and other products. Two apps handle the large majority of transactions, a concentration regulators have long wanted to reduce but have repeatedly postponed acting on.

Neither problem stops the curve rising. Both will shape whether the system can pay for the security, fraud prevention and resilience that a network of this size needs.

value.title: Key points
points: UPI processed about 185 billion transactions in 2024-25, up from under a billion in 2017-18.
Growth is driven by many small payments; the average value per payment keeps falling.
Zero fees for most payments leave the system dependent on subsidies and cross-selling.

articles.headline: India's cities have heat plans. Most are not built to work
articles.standfirst: Ahmedabad showed in 2013 that a heat action plan can save lives. A decade on, dozens of cities have one, but few have the money, local data or legal backing to make it more than a document.
articles.hero_caption: An illustration of a city street shimmering in heat, with a water stall shaded by a striped awning.
articles.hero_alt: Illustration of a hot city street and a shaded water stall.

body.value:
After a heatwave in May 2010 caused a sharp rise in deaths, Ahmedabad drew up South Asia's first heat action plan in 2013. The idea was simple: warn people early, open cooling spaces, keep water available, change working hours for outdoor labour, and prepare hospitals for heatstroke. Studies afterwards suggested it saved lives. The plan became a template, and national disaster-management guidelines now encourage every heat-prone city and state to have one.

Many do. The trouble is what is inside them.
Plans without teeth

A 2023 review by the Centre for Policy Research of 37 heat action plans found that most were built on national rather than local temperature thresholds, few identified the people most at risk, and almost none said where the money would come from. Many did not name which department was legally responsible for each action. A plan that cannot be funded or enforced is a list of good intentions.

Heat also does its damage at night. Warm nights, when the body cannot recover, are increasingly common in Indian cities, yet most plans are triggered only by daytime maximum temperatures. Humidity, which makes the same temperature far more dangerous in coastal cities, is often ignored.

value.quote: A heatwave is a disaster that leaves no rubble, which is why it is so easy to under-prepare for.

value.title: Key points
points: Ahmedabad's 2013 plan, the first in South Asia, became the model for others.
A 2023 review of 37 plans found most lacked local thresholds, vulnerability mapping and funding.
Night-time heat and humidity are often left out of the triggers.
The fix is local data, named responsibilities and a budget line.

body.value: What to watch

Look for three changes in the plans cities publish before next summer: thresholds set from local health and weather data, a list of the people most at risk (outdoor workers, the elderly, slum residents), and a budget. Where all three appear, the plan is likely to save lives. Where they do not, it is likely to be rediscovered only after the next heatwave.

sources.title: How is India adapting to heatwaves? An assessment of heat action plans

about_page.title: About us
about_page.intro: Manthan Reviews is an analysis-led publication about India and its place in the world. We publish news, analysis, explainers, opinion and editorials, and we care more about context than speed. Please note that the site is currently running demonstration content: the articles and authors you see are illustrative examples written to show how the publication works, not reports of real events.

body.value: Who we are

Manthan Reviews is an independent newsroom built on a simple idea: that readers are better served by understanding a story than by merely hearing about it first. We cover politics, the economy, business, data, cities, society, the environment, education, health, science, sport, culture and India's relations with the world, and we try to explain not just what happened but why it matters and what might happen next.

We are a small team of reporters, editors and columnists drawn from across the country. We have no affiliation with any political party, and our editorial decisions are made by our editors alone.
Why Manthan

Manthan means churning. In the old story of the churning of the ocean, gods and demons heave on a great serpent wound around a mountain, and out of the turbulence come poison and nectar alike. News works the same way. Every day brings a flood of claims, numbers and noise; our job is to churn it patiently until what is valuable rises to the top, and to tell you plainly which is which.

value.title: Demonstration content
value.body: This site currently runs demonstration content. Bylines belong to fictional writers, people quoted are illustrative, and articles are written to show our formats and standards rather than to report specific real events. Real institutions are mentioned for context only, and nothing here should be cited as fact.

body.value: Our editorial standards
Every article we publish is reviewed by at least one editor before it goes live. We hold ourselves to a few non-negotiable principles:

value.title: Our principles
points: Accuracy first: we check facts, figures and quotations before publication, and we say so when something cannot be verified.
Clear sourcing: we link to primary documents and official data wherever possible, and list our main sources at the end of each article.
Fairness: people and organisations we write about critically are given a reasonable opportunity to respond.
Anonymity is the exception: we grant it only when a source would face real harm for speaking, and we describe their role as precisely as we can.
Separation of news and opinion: our reporting does not take sides; our opinion pages and editorials are clearly labelled.

body.value: Article types

Every article carries a label so that you know what kind of journalism you are reading.

  • News reports what has happened, as fully and fairly as we can establish it.
  • Analysis goes behind the news to explain causes, consequences and trade-offs. It reflects the reporter's informed judgement but not a political position.
  • Explainer sets out the background to a complex subject, often in question-and-answer form, so that readers can follow the debate.
  • Opinion is a signed argument by a columnist or guest writer. It represents the writer's view, not Manthan Reviews'.
  • Editorial is the unsigned, collective view of our editorial board, and the only place where Manthan Reviews itself takes a position.
How we use AI

Our articles are produced by AI agents working under human editors, and every one is approved by an editor before it is published. Our AI policy explains what the agents do and what they never do. To report a mistake, see our corrections policy; for anything else, contact us.
